title: Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown (2011)
summary: A foreign subsidiary is not subject to general jurisdiction in North Carolina because some of its tires reach the state through affiliated distributors; all-purpose jurisdiction requires affiliations so continuous and systematic that the corporation is essentially at home, paradigmatically its place of incorporation and principal place of business.
notes:
The course’s later Daimler and BNSF materials develop the at-home inquiry. Perkins and Helicopteros receive separate indexed accounts here, even though the syllabus assigns them through Goodyear’s discussion.

Two 13-year-old boys from North Carolina died in a bus crash outside Paris attributed to a tire made in Turkey; the defendants were Goodyear USA and its subsidiaries in Turkey, France and Luxembourg, and Justice Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Court, framing the paradigm general-jurisdiction forums as the place of incorporation and the principal place of business.

sections.Parties: The parents of Julian Brown and Matthew Helms, North Carolina residents, sued as administrators of their sons’ estates. The defendants were The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company, an Ohio corporation, and three indirect subsidiaries organized and operating in Luxembourg, Turkey and France. Only the three foreign subsidiaries contested personal jurisdiction and petitioned for certiorari; the American parent operated in North Carolina and did not challenge the state courts’ authority over it, and its presence did not establish jurisdiction over each separately incorporated subsidiary.
sections.Material Facts: In April 2004 the two boys, thirteen-year-old soccer players, died in a bus accident outside Paris on the way to the airport. Their parents alleged that a defective tire made at the Turkish subsidiary’s plant caused the crash and challenged its design, construction, testing and inspection. The accident, the manufacture of the tire and its sale all occurred outside North Carolina, and the tire was a type not distributed there. The subsidiaries made tires mainly for European and Asian markets, had no North Carolina place of business, employees, bank accounts or registration, and did not design, sell or ship tires there. Some of their other tires nevertheless reached the state through other Goodyear affiliates: tens of thousands out of tens of millions made, many special-order.
sections.Procedural History: The parents filed wrongful-death claims in the Superior Court for Onslow County, and the subsidiaries’ motions to dismiss were denied. The North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed, 199 N.C. App. 50 (2009): it conceded that specific jurisdiction was unavailable because the injury did not arise from North Carolina contacts, but found general jurisdiction because the subsidiaries had placed tires into an organized distribution system that carried some to North Carolina and had not taken steps to prevent it, stressing the state’s interest in a forum for its residents. The North Carolina Supreme Court denied review. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed, refusing to consider the parents’ single-enterprise theory because they had not raised it below or in opposing certiorari.
sections.Issue: Does a foreign subsidiary become subject to general personal jurisdiction in North Carolina because some tires it manufactures abroad enter the state through affiliated distribution channels, when the lawsuit concerns a different tire and a fatal accident in France? May contacts that might support specific jurisdiction over a product claim instead support adjudication of any claim against the manufacturer?
sections.Holding: No. Justice Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Court. A state may exercise general, all-purpose jurisdiction over a corporation only when its affiliations with the state are so continuous and systematic as to render it essentially at home there; the paradigm homes are the place of incorporation and the principal place of business, with Perkins illustrating a sufficiently central operation elsewhere. The subsidiaries’ limited, indirect tire distribution did not make them at home in North Carolina, so the state could not hear these unrelated claims.
sections.Reasoning: The Court began with the difference between a forum’s power over a particular dispute and its power over every dispute involving a defendant. Product distribution can create a contact relevant to a claim about that product’s presence or use in the forum; it does not create a corporate home, and treating the circulation of products as sufficient for general jurisdiction would make any substantial manufacturer answerable on any claim wherever its goods were sold. The North Carolina courts had imported stream-of-commerce reasoning into the wrong inquiry, and the plaintiffs had conceded that the forum transactions were unconnected to the accident. Their sons’ residence gave them a strong reason to want a local forum but added nothing to the subsidiaries’ own affiliations with the state. Measured against Perkins, where the president ran a Philippine company from Ohio, and Helicopteros, where substantial Texas purchases and training trips did not suffice, the subsidiaries fell far short. The parent’s operations did not erase the subsidiaries’ separate identities, and because the single-enterprise theory was forfeited the Court did not decide when affiliates’ contacts may be attributed to one another.

learning.why: North Carolina could not exercise all-purpose jurisdiction over foreign subsidiaries on claims arising from a bus accident in France.

topics.general-jurisdiction: The foreign subsidiaries’ limited North Carolina distribution did not make them essentially at home there.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: A corporate family does not eliminate the need to identify the sued entities’ own jurisdictional position.
topics.cp-stream-commerce: A product’s distribution can support a suit-related inquiry without supporting all-purpose jurisdiction.
topics.specific-jurisdiction: The opinion drew the modern line between specific and general jurisdiction and rejected stream-of-commerce contacts as a basis for the latter.
